reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: An X-linked recessive lower motor neuron disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the androgen receptor gene, so it affects men while female carriers are usually spared or minimally affected
Presents in adult men with slowly progressive proximal limb weakness, muscle cramps, and prominent bulbar involvement causing dysarthria and dysphagia
Fasciculations, especially of the face, chin, and perioral muscles, and postural or action tremor are characteristic clues
Because the androgen receptor is affected, signs of partial androgen insensitivity such as gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, and reduced fertility are common
There are no upper motor neuron signs, which helps distinguish it from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Sensory involvement can be demonstrated electrophysiologically even when clinically subtle, reflecting an associated sensory neuronopathy
Serum creatine kinase is often elevated, and metabolic features such as impaired glucose tolerance may accompany the disorder
Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting the expanded CAG repeat in the androgen receptor gene
reference.pathophysiology: Kennedy disease is a polyglutamine disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome. The elongated polyglutamine tract renders the mutant, ligand-bound androgen receptor prone to misfolding and nuclear accumulation, which is toxic to lower motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord and to dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons. The androgen-dependent toxicity explains why the phenotype is expressed in males and why partial androgen insensitivity features accompany the neuronopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (particularly lower motor neuron predominant forms)
Spinal muscular atrophy of adult onset
Chronic inflammatory or immune-mediated motor neuropathies
Inclusion body myositis and other myopathies with proximal weakness and dysphagia
Myasthenic and other neuromuscular junction disorders with bulbar features
additionalInvestigations: Androgen receptor CAG repeat analysis as the confirmatory test
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showing chronic denervation and sensory involvement
Endocrine and metabolic evaluation including glucose tolerance and androgen status
Swallowing assessment to guide aspiration risk management
redFlags: Progressive dysphagia with aspiration and weight loss
Choking episodes or compromised airway protection
Rapid deterioration suggesting an alternative or superimposed diagnosis
Emergence of upper motor neuron signs prompting reconsideration of ALS
reference.prognosis: The disorder progresses slowly over many years, and life expectancy is often near normal, though bulbar weakness can lead to aspiration and disability; mobility and swallowing decline gradually and management is supportive.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and giving an unduly poor prognosis
Overlooking the endocrine and metabolic features that support the diagnosis
Underestimating aspiration risk from bulbar involvement
Not offering genetic counselling to at-risk male relatives and carrier daughters
